The strengths are:
1) the theory is a new perspective for analyzing the effect of clipping.

2) the proposed global clipping achieved some gains over commonly used gradient clipping.

The weaknesses are:
1) The new theory does not uncover anything new compared with existing analyses on gradient clipping which computes the bias on gradient estimators when equipped with clipping. And the proposed analysis is even more complicated because it requires analyzing positive semi-definiteness of NTK matrix. In addition, the theory only covers GD while the more interested cases is SGD and it is not straightforward how the result will change when extended to SGD. Thus, the value of the new theory is not well justified.

2) The proposed global clipping method is a new heuristic to limit l2 sensitivity of gradient estimators, however, why it leads to better calibration is unclear.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the comments. We would like to highlight that global clipping is a novel method that resembles SGD or SGLD when $R$ is large. Because SGLD is the most popular way to train Bayesian neural network, which by definition is calibrated, we expect and empirically observe that DP-SGD with global clipping leads to better calibration.

Besides our contribution of a new clipping method, the phenomenon of calibration issue in DP regime is completely new. Besides, our Fact 4.1 gives a unified framework that includes DP-SGD of all clipping methods (local, global and more) and non-DP SGD. This framework itself can serve as future tool to study noise-free DP-SGD (only in the continuous time).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper analyzes the impact of DP training (noise addition and clipping) on the training dynamics through gradient flow (i.e., assuming small learning rate) and the change of the NTK matrix. From the analysis, the paper finds that noise addition has a negligible impact on training convergence, but clipping destroys the loss convergence guarantee (especially for layerwise clipping where even convergence does not guarantee 0 loss). Then, the paper proposes global clipping which zeros-out the gradient with large norm ($g_i \ge c$), and empirically demonstrates the benefits of this global clipping strategy in terms of loss minimization and calibration.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper provides a succinct but important understanding of the DP training regime which characterizes and isolates the impacts of each ingredient. The NTK and gradient flow tool is not new. However, it seems novel to apply the tool to DP training analysis which provides meaningful insights.
2. Global clipping is shown effective in practice. Moreover, this change in the clipping method may highlight the ignored design choices from the clipping perspective in DP training. A good contribution to the community.

Weaknesses:
1. The presentation can be improved - the theoretical understanding and the proposal of global clipping seems quite disconnected and the paper seems to be gluing these two parts together. It would be great if we can incorporate threotical analysis of the global clipping. For example, the authors may think about how the zeroing-out of some diagonal $C$ elements changes the eigenvalues of the NTK matrix?

2. The theoretical part seems to be not very technically involved and the analysis mainly delivers a qualitative result of the convergence instead of the analysis of convergence rate, etc.

Minor:
1. When mentioning Algorithm 2 on Page 5, please specify its location in the appendices.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a variant of DP-SGD for training ML models under differential privacy. The method is based on a notion of global clipping, where the norm of each stochastic gradient is treated by the same clipping factor. This differs from the local clipping methods previously in the literature. The paper provides analysis of DP training dynamics under the NTK framework. On the experimental side, it is observed that DP-SGD with global clipping outperforms prior methods with local clipping in terms of convergence and calibration.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
----
The paper proposes a new gradient clipping method for DP-SGD. This is a novel idea and could lead to practical impact. The method is simple and can be easily incorporated into the existing DP ML engineering frameworks. 

The paper studies calibration of DP trained neural networks, which I think is a fresh angle.

The paper is generally well-written, and the main ideas are presented cleanly. 

The paper provides experimental validations of their algorithms, over various datasets and network architectures. The details are clear. 

Weaknesses
----

On the algorithmic side, one concern is the sample complexity implication of using global clipping. Specifically, the clipping hyperparameter $R$ (also denoted by $C$ in other papers) of DP-SGD with per-sample clipping is typically chosen to be the median norm of the gradients.  (“In practice, a good way to choose a value for C is by taking the median of the norms of the unclipped gradients over the course of training.” from https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00133). However, if we do that in global clipping, we are effectively discarding half of the dataset. Intuitively, that sounds wasteful. Then to compensate for that, I can choose $R$ to be larger than the median for global clipping. This is indeed the case in some of the experiments of this paper: notice that in Figure 7 and part of Figure 9, R_global is chosen to be much larger than R_local. However, the trade-off would be a higher noise level during training, which should hurt utility. Somehow I do not see this issue manifesting itself in the experiments. 

For the experiments, again, R_global is sometimes chosen to be different, in fact, much larger than R_local. Isn’t it more fair to make the same? Can the author(s) provide more details on how they tune the hyperparameters? What is the maximum gradient norm in each experiment, and the quantile where R_global and R_local lie?

I also have a few concerns about the theoretical analysis in section 4. 

* First, I question the claim that DP-GD is “the most widely used”. Moreover, the prior section focuses on a variant of DP-SGD with global clipping. As a result, I think it’s natural and important to analyze the convergence of DP-SGD$_{global}$. Looking at the Appendix F, the analysis of other methods also apply only to gradient-flow-type algorithms, such as gradient flow with momentum. In other words, the paper proposes algorithm A (i.e., DP-SGD with global clipping); yet its analysis is on some other algorithm B (DP gradient flow). I believe the theory part can be strengthened by bridging this gap and by analyzing (batch) DP-SGD methods. 

* I want to point out that the NTK analysis, in general, does not correspond perfectly to the behavior of real neural networks. NTK-based analysis assumes small step size (gradient flow) and infinite width. This is known as the lazy training regime and practical DL do not always lie in this regime.  

* Theorem 1 appears as a bit weak. Statement 1 and 2 only say that DP-SGD with per-sample (i.e., local) clipping breaks the PSD-ness of the NTK matrix. However, quantitatively, how does that affect convergence rate (or any other property of the training process)? I understand that Figure 9 and 10 try to demonstrate slower convergence *in experiments*, but the theory doesn’t really say that. Statement 3 claims that the loss *may* not reduce monotonically. It is unclear whether this is a problem in practice. After all, I may only care about the final loss. For the first part of Statement 4, I think the proof in the appendix is incomplete. In particular, one needs to show that $L=0$. However, in page 14 of the appendix, it is only shown that $\mathrm{d} f = 0$. 

* I don’t see Theorem 2 as a particularly interesting statement. As the author(s) acknowledge, local and global clipping are both equivalent to no clipping for sufficiently large $R$ (that is, $R\geq \text{every gradient norm}$). Without any clipping, though, DP-SGD does not yield good training performance in practice, since the noise level of the Gaussian mechanism is too high.

* In general, does the theory suggest that nontrivial global clipping is superior to to local clipping, in any quantitative way? (If I am not misunderstanding Theorem 2 is really for a trivial global clipping procedure (i.e., no clipping).)

The work could do a better job on surveying related literature. For DP training on CIFAR-10, the paper cites Papernot et al. (2020) as the state-of-the-art. I am not sure that is the case anymore. There has been several more recent work claiming stronger DP training results. For instance, “Unlocking High-Accuracy Differentially Private Image Classification through Scale” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.13650) by Soham De, Leonard Berrada, Jamie Hayes, Samuel L. Smith, Borja Balle and “Practical and Private (Deep) Learning without Sampling or Shuffling” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00039) by Peter Kairouz, Brendan McMahan, Shuang Song, Om Thakkar, Abhradeep Thakurta, Zheng Xu. 

For the experiments on CIFAR-10, I suggest the author(s) to compare with De et al. [2022] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.13650).

Other minor comments
---
1. Abstract: “We successfully characterize the effects” — remove “successfully”
2. Page 2: “For example, state-of-the-art CIFAR10 accuracy with DP is ≈ 70% without pre-training” — this is for what privacy loss $\epsilon$?
3. Algorithm 1: “with probability p” —> “each sample with probability p” 
4. Statement of Theorem 1 and 2, $f$ refers to the output of the neural network?
5. For Figure 10: there is only one $R$. Is the clipping norm set to be the same for local and global method?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I appreciate the clarity, simplicity and the scope of experiments of this work. To the best of my knowledge, the main algorithmic idea is novel.  However, there is room for strengthening the theory part of the work. I have made several suggestions above.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a novel and simple idea for DP training of ML models. While idea seems validated by some experiments,  the theory aspects of the paper may require more work. Therefore, I do not recommend accept.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments!

Comment: R_global is sometimes chosen to be different, in fact, much larger than R_local. Isn’t it more fair to make the same? ...... What is the maximum gradient norm in each experiment, and the quantile where R_global and R_local lie?

**Response:** We will conduct new experiment in the next submission to compare this. We don't compute the quantile (e.g. median) because this quantity is also data-driven and requires extra privacy budget to use it as a guideline for choosing the clipping norm.

Comment: In other words, the paper proposes algorithm A (i.e., DP-SGD with global clipping); yet its analysis is on some other algorithm B (DP gradient flow). I believe the theory part can be strengthened by bridging this gap and by analyzing (batch) DP-SGD methods.

**Response:** We agree that it would be more desirable to work with DP-SGD than DP-GD as the former is more popular in practice. However, even in the non-DP regime, SGD is much more difficult to analyze (usually requires different assumptions and technical tools) than GD. An example in NTK regime may be (Simon S. Du, Jason D. Lee, Haochuan Li, Liwei Wang, and Xiyu Zhai. Gradient descent finds global minima of deep neural networks); or, in non-convex optimization regime, SGD usually proves that the oracle gradient norm converges to 0 (see S. Ghadimi, G. Lan, and H. Zhang. Mini-batch stochastic approximation methods for nonconvex stochastic composite optimization), instead of the loss convergence by GD.

Comment: NTK analysis, in general, does not correspond perfectly to the behavior of real neural networks. NTK-based analysis assumes small step size (gradient flow) and infinite width. This is known as the lazy training regime and practical DL do not always lie in this regime.

**Response:** We totally agree and therefore we are not conducting the classic NTK analysis. We are merely using the concept of NTK matrix to study monotonicity of convergence, which **does not require lazy training nor infinite width**. Please see footnote 1.

Comment: As the author(s) acknowledge, local and global clipping are both equivalent to no clipping for sufficiently large R. Without any clipping, though, DP-SGD does not yield good training performance in practice, since the noise level of the Gaussian mechanism is too high.

**Response:** We will elaborate on the difference between local and global clipping when R is large, in the next submission. However, it is worth noticing that recent advances have shown that large batch size can effectively (though not completely) remove the negative effect of large Gaussian noise level.

Comment: The work could do a better job on surveying related literature. For DP training on CIFAR-10, the paper cites Papernot et al. (2020) as the state-of-the-art. I am not sure that is the case anymore.

**Response:** We think Papernot et al. still present (at least one of) SOTA when model is trained from scratch (i.e. without pretraining). There are a few better results like De et al. but they rely on heavy pretraining on ImageNet.

Overall, thank you for the suggestions!

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper suggests a new "global" gradient clipping method for differentially private optimization. It is analyzed theoretically for an NTK model and shown to have better properties than the original "local" clipping. Experimental results show certain benefits of the proposed approach for several image and text problems in terms of optimization and calibration.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths 

The work is well-motivated and presents a study of an important and non-trivial problem. The literature overview seems accurate and the paper is well-organized.

Numerical results are quite extensive but seem to be rather detached from the theoretical analysis as calibration was not analyzed mathematically and appears suddenly in the experimental section. Although empirical analysis of calibration for models trained with DP-SGD seems novel.

## Weaknesses

**1.** I find several claims from the paper not justified. 
- First, according to the **Our Contributions** paragraph:
> the noise only affects the privacy but not the convergence.

This claim is either wrong or not well-formulated because stochastic noise can clearly affect the convergence of the (stochastic) gradient descent-type method. This can be observed from proper convergence analysis [1, 2] (and lower bounds [3]) of SGD with constant step size for convex/non-convex settings.

- Second, in Section 2 the authors 
> review the standard, non-DP Gradient Descent (GD) for **arbitrary neural network** and **arbitrary loss** that can be represented as a sum of per-sample losses.

This sentence is simply not mathematically valid as an **arbitrary** neural network can have non-smooth activations which are not even differentiable, so the gradient descent is not really applicable. In addition, I find it misleading considering the fact that further throughout the paper convexity of $f$ and positive definiteness of ${\mathbf H}(t)$ is assumed. This model can not represent the training of an **arbitrary** neural network as it is a very simplified model and this needs to be stated clearly.

**2.** The proposed "global" clipping may not work for very simple examples. Consider a one-dimensional quadratic optimization problem  of function
$$ 
f(x) = 0.5 a x^2 - b x, 
$$
for $a>0, b \neq 0$, which is minimized for $x^\star = b/a$. For such simple problem Gradient Descent with the suggested clipping operator will never converge to the true solution if initialized from point $x^0 = 0$ and $R>b$. I believe that this simple intuition can be generalized as the method just ignores gradients with norms larger than the clipping factor. 

___


[1] Gower, Robert Mansel, et al. "SGD: General analysis and improved rates." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2019.


[2] Khaled, Ahmed, and Peter Richtárik. "Better theory for SGD in the nonconvex world." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.03329 (2020).


[3] Ding, Zhiyan, et al. "Error lower bounds of constant step-size stochastic gradient descent." arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.08212 (2019).

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2718 by Reviewer 2Z8K

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed comments! We enjoyed the technical discussion and will address your concerns one by one:

1. Comment: This claim ("the noise only affects the privacy but not the convergence.") is either wrong or not well-formulated because stochastic noise can clearly affect the convergence of the (stochastic) gradient descent-type method. This can be observed from proper convergence analysis [1, 2] (and lower bounds [3]) of SGD with constant step size for convex/non-convex settings.

Response: Our statement is rigorous and correct, but have to understood in the whole sentence, which we quote "......**in the continuous
time analysis**, showing that the clipping only affects the convergence but not the privacy, and that the noise only affects the privacy but not the convergence." As we argued in the paper, continuous time means infinitely small learning rate. Therefore the continuous time behavior is a simplified version of that of discrete time, which has been widely used in theoretical analysis. To close the gap between continuous and discrete time convergence, we also provide Fact 4.1 (with proof in appendix) and empirical evidence in Figure 3. 

2. Comment: This sentence is simply not mathematically valid as an arbitrary neural network can have non-smooth activations which are not even differentiable, so the gradient descent is not really applicable. 

Response: As far as we are concerned, neural networks with non-smooth activations are still learned by gradient descent (happy to take counter-examples). Regarding differentiability, it suffices to have sub-differentiability **in practice**, e.g. ReLU(x) is not everywhere differentiable (it is differentiable except at x=0), but people have no trouble using sign(x) as a sub-gradient in deep learning.

3. Comment: In addition, I find it misleading considering the fact that further throughout the paper convexity of $f$ and positive definiteness of H(t) is assumed. This model can not represent the training of an arbitrary neural network as it is a very simplified model and this needs to be stated clearly.

Response: We **never** assume the convexity of neural network $f$! If you read carefully, we assume that the loss is convex with respect to the network output. This is satisfied by most losses, e.g. cross entropy and MSE, with $l_1/l_2$ penalty, etc. Regarding the positive definiteness of H(t), it is a common assumption in the NTK regime (see footnote 1).

4. Comment: The proposed "global" clipping may not work for very simple examples (like $f(x)=0.5ax^2-bx$).

Response: What an interesting example! Let us first set a=1 since it's not used anywhere. Then the gradient is $x-b$ and **our global clipping indeed works** when $x_0=0, R>b$. What you meant should be it does not work when $x_0=0, R<b$. The interesting part is that global clipping include the non-DP training when $R=\infty, \sigma=0$. In short, whenever non-DP gradient descent works, with large R, global clipping always works.

5. Comment: what kind of convergence is shown in Proof of Fact 4.1 as the discrete dynamics has a random variable on the right-hand side?

Response: Fact 4.1 is not about convergence. It's about deriving the continuous time dynamics from the discrete time dynamics.

6. Comment: I would like to clarify why matrix C is assumed to be positive. Why doesn't it have zero entries in case the clipping happens?

Response: Positive does not mean strictly positive here. Some entries of C can be zero.

7. Comment: Were they tuned individually or how the choice was performed? How well can the proposed technique be compatible with adaptive [4] clipping?

Response: It is a common approach to use small clipping norm in DP deep learning (for local clipping). However, we found for global clipping, large clipping norm is better. So yes, they are individually tuned. Finally, **global clipping is compatible with adaptive clipping** because they are two directions of clipping. Global clipping is a per-sample gradient clipping function; adaptive clipping is a choice of clipping norm that can work with any clipping function.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
The paper contains an interesting mathematical analysis of the phenomena, with a good theoretical investigation and convincing experiments. It situates the research well within the scientific context and has an extensive bibliography.

## Weaknesses
The paper is hard to read and incomplete. The main findings seem moot on the basis of the the experimental results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity
The paper misses Algorithm 2 (referenced before eq4.4), Figure 14 (referenced at the end of sec6.2), and relies crucially on the Appendices in the supplementary material. 

Fig 2 is terrible:
* it silently assumes that the per-sample gradient vector (it would be useful to recall that is $v_t^{(i)}$) is one-dimensional and orthogonal (why?)
* the representation of noise addition is weird at best; why not make the arrow or its head fuzzy for instance?
* I'm not clear why small R/red circles is applied to local only, resp. large/grey on global?
(I would recommend keeping the order local/global from Algo 1, label the rows with "local" and "global", and the columns with the symbols used in Algo 1, $v_t^{(i)}$, $\bar{V}_t$ etc)

## Quality
Before eq4.3: "the flat clipping upper bounds the entire gradient vector by a norm $R$": if we're speaking of $\bar{V}_t$, this is not bounded by $R$, for instance for flat local clipping, $n=2$ and two equal per-sample gradients $v_t^{(i)}$, if I understood well, $||\bar{V}_t||_2 = 2R$. 

I'm unclear how Fig 9 and 10 depict loss convergence failing for non-pos-def NTK: in Fig 9, shouldn't the global layer case converge to 0 per Theorem 1, point 4 ? Plot Fig 10 left does not give me a clear sense that the loss is not converging.

The paper does not analyse how moving from discrete-time to continuous-time for the analysis impacts its conclusions. I am looking forward to author response on weaknesses I outline.

The analysis seems novel. 

## Reproducibility
Thanks to references to tutorials for CIFAR10 and SNLI experiments, it might be feasible to reproduce these results, but many details are missing from the paper. I have not checked the supplementary material to figure out whether it provides sufficient details for reproduction. Code is not linked or mentioned in the main paper. The regression task is very sketchily described.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for reading the paper and the suggestions! However, we are sorry that the reviewer fails to understand our DP optimization with per-sample gradient clipping. The comments make several factual mistakes which we clarify here.

*Mistaken comment 1:* Fig 2 "silently assumes that the per-sample gradient vector is one-dimensional and orthogonal (why?)

Response: We don't assume the per-sample gradient is orthogonal nor any angular assumption, e.g. there are clearly 3 black arrows (3 per-sample gradients) in Figure 2 first column. And clearly these per-sample gradient vectors are two-dimensional.

*Mistaken comment 2:* Before eq4.3: "the flat clipping upper bounds the entire gradient vector by a norm R": if we're speaking of $\bar{V}_t$, this is not bounded by R.

Response: 'Flat clipping' is a well-known terminology and we have stated very clearly that the "entire gradient" means entire per-sample gradient. It should be obvious that the gradient clipping is with respect to per-sample gradient, whose norm is upper bounded by R.
This is also clear in the context: in eq 4.3, we denote the per-sample gradient as $\nabla_w l_j$ to mean the $j$-th per-sample gradient. 

*Mistaken comment 3:* I'm unclear how Fig 9 and 10 depict loss convergence failing for non-pos-def NTK: in Fig 9, shouldn't the global layer case converge to 0 per Theorem 1, point 4 ? 

Response: In Fig 8, the global layerwise clipping indeed converges to 0 per Theorem 1, point 4. The loss of global clipping is monotonically decreasing but that of local clipping (non-pos-def NTK) is not. We are confused by this comment.

*Mistaken comment 4:* Plot Fig 10 left does not give me a clear sense that the loss is not converging.

Response: The loss of existing clipping is clearly DIVERGING!
